rv.q: Mr. Weiler eschews high drama and flashy histrionics in favor of a keen focus on the workings of the hearts and minds of his characters.
The more I realized that Serio and Weiler had diverted me with teenage drama from an adult horror beneath, the more I admired the 90 minutes I spent at the Atlantic.
It’s a message that bears repeating now and again, and it’s seldom rendered more accessibly or beautifully than it is here.

rv.q: The new play from Bubba Weiler is another can't-miss excavation of the heart.
The play is something of a miracle, both in the terrain it covers and the way it manages to do so without constricting itself to convention or condescension.
That each member of this quartet is achingly vulnerable only adds to the impact of this quiet stunner.
Their latest collaboration yields The Saviors, yet another compelling drama and fine production that deserve a longer existence.
If there’s a message to the play, it’s that these words are ones to live by -- no matter your religion (or lack thereof)!
Ivan Howe and Julius Rinzel give breathtakingly realized performances, keenly detailing the shifts in their friendship and attitudes towards their faith.
What’s most exciting about “The Saviors,” a play ostensibly about two altar boys, is the feeling that you are witnessing the literal early stages of several major talents.
The ensemble is a total pleasure and gives the story everything they have.
What keeps this drama moving at rapid speed is Weiler’s gift for comic dialogue.
The Saviors' lapses can easily be fixed with a second draft of this intriguing but not quite there play.
Sounds like a somber affair, but in the hands of the talented cast and director Jack Serio, it's actually quite the opposite.
Weiler has emerged as one of the most precociously promising playwrights of the American theater.
The result is that 'The Saviors' survives not because it works, but because it has enough structural integrity that an engaged audience can excavate what the production obscures.
The ending is an unresolved cop-out. Individual stories don't connect well. Empathy comes and goes without sustaining. The piece has unrealized potential.

cn.t: Weiler's tender follow-up to his acclaimed debut explores faith and friendship through two altar boys, earning praise for its emotional depth and remarkable performances by age-appropriate teen actors, though some critics find it less impactful than his first play.

vr.q: It is a deeply beautiful and honest and painful coming of age friendship play, and you should go see it because I haven't stopped thinking about it.
I was charmed by the actors' performances, and I was warmed by this depiction of boys who are trying so earnestly to be good
